pas un plâtre.

La réduction de l'immobilisation permet également la mobilité précoce, permettant l'accélération de la reprise de

fonction à moyen terme et donc de la reprise des activités, limitant les complications et favorisant le recrutement

cortical. Tout cela doit bien sûr être médié par l'irritabilité du patient.

La rééducation strictement passive est moins intéressante que l'actif-aidé et l'actif à faible intensité : < 15 à 20% de la

contraction maximale volontaire (Edwards et al, 2017, 10.2519/jospt.2017.7271, Thigpen, 2016,

10.1016/j.jse.2015.12.018). Il est souhaitable et sur d'encourager L'ACTIF ET L'ACTIF AIDE dès J1 en tenant compte

du geste chirurgical, de l'irritabilité du patient, et de son adhésion aux exercices) et cela jusqu'à 6 semaines

(Gallagher, 2015, 10.1080/00913847.2015.1025683, Mazuquin, 2021, 10.1371/journal.pone.0252137)

Il manque pour moi la phase de 6 à 12 semaines, centrée sur l'augmentation des amplitudes, la chaîne cinétique, le

contrôle neuromoteur, la récupération de l'élévation active et de toutes les mobilités passives, la stimulation des

muscles de la coiffe, le deltoïde, le trapèze inférieur et le dentelé antérieur et bien que l'ajout de résistance commence

à 3 mois, la possibilité d'ajouter pesanteur, endurance et vitesse jusqu'à 50% de la contraction maximale volontaire

(Edwards et al, 2017, 10.2519/jospt.2017.7271, Thigpen, 2016, 10.1016/j.jse.2015.12.018).

La restauration complète de la mobilité n'est à mon sens pas un prérequis total au départ de la phase de récupération

fonctionnelle active contre résistance légère à 3 mois. De plus, le terme de "mobilisation contre résistance" ne me

parait pas adapté, renvoyant toujours à une certaine notion de passivité. La phase débutant à 3 mois et UNE PHASE

ACTIVE potentiellement avec des mobilisations à visée de gain d'amplitude si nécessaire. Concernant les travailleurs

manuels et/ou sportifs, la phase de préparation du retour au travail/retour au sport/réathlétisation commence avant 6

mois (Altintas, 2020, 10.1177/0363546519825624, Shimada, 2020, 10.1177/2325967120922203)

Durée d'immobilisation : https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24382719/ « Early ROM » vs immobilisation 6 semaines :

pas de différence de guérison tendineuse (92 % global), meilleure élévation/exo à 3 mois dans le groupe mobilisation

précoce.

Mazzocca et al., JSES 2017 (prospective)

Patients avec réparation sous faible tension autorisés à commencer actif assisté dès la 2e semaine.

Pas plus de ruptures constatées à 1 an; meilleure élévation active précoce.

Lee et al., Am J Sports Med 2012 (RCT, n=107)

Comparé :

Actif précoce (exercices actifs dès J3)

vs Actif retardé (6 semaines d’immobilisation)

À 12 mois : scores fonctionnels équivalents, pas plus de re-tear dans le groupe actif précoce (15 % vs 17 %).

Avantage : récupération plus rapide de la fonction à 3 mois.

Le délai d'immobilisation est trop long ici. 6 semaines ne me parait pas adapté.

Il est en réalité plutôt de 3 ou 4 semaines.

Possibilité d'une phase de "restauration": on ne comprend pas le sens.

Réathlétisation de l'épaule à partir de 6 mois pour les patients W manuel ou les patients sportifs.

Analyse présentée par question

Analyse effectuée sur l'ensemble des questionnaires validés.

Projet : Prise en charge des tendinopathies rompues de la coiffe des rotateurs : place de la chirurgie

Questionnaire : Modèles de comptes-rendus d'imagerie

Nombre d'experts sélectionnés : 55 personne(s)

Nombre de questionnaires validés : 45 questionnaire(s)

Taux de participation : 81.81%

Nous  vous  remercions  d'avoir  accepté  de  participer  au  groupe  de  lecture  relatif  à  la  «  Prise  en  charge  des

tendinopathies  rompues  de  la  coiffe  des  rotateurs  :  place  de  la  chirurgie  ».  Vous  trouverez  ci-dessous  le

questionnaire concernant les modèles de compte-rendu d'imagerie. Votre mission consiste : à lire le texte des

recommandations,  l'argumentaire,  les  modèles  de  comptes-rendus  et  la  fiche  synthétique  à  donner  un  avis

sur la lisibilité, la faisabilité et l'applicabilité de ces modèles de comptes-rendus d'imagerie en cotant chaque

proposition  de  recommandations  à  l'aide  de  l'échelle  de  cotation  et  en  apportant  des  arguments

complémentaires  ou  contradictoires  (sous  forme  de  commentaires  libres)  reposant  si  possible  sur  la

littérature, et sur votre expertise lorsque la littérature est insuffisante ou inexistante. Nous vous invitons à lire

l'ensemble des documents avant de remplir le questionnaire, afin d'avoir une vision globale. De même, nous

vous invitons à répondre en respectant l'ordre du questionnaire (lecture verticale du questionnaire) en raison

de  l'interrelation  existante  entre  les  différentes  propositions  des  chapitres.  Pour  la  phase  de  cotation,  en

regard de chaque proposition du questionnaire est placée une échelle numérique discontinue graduée de « 1

»  à  « 9 ».  La  cotation doit être  fondée  sur les  données  de la littérature  et votre  expérience dans le  domaine

abordé.  La  valeur  «  1  »  signifie  que  la  proposition  n'est  pas  du  tout  conforme  aux  données  actuelles  de  la

littérature et que vous êtes en désaccord total avec la proposition, La valeur « 9 » signifie que la proposition

est tout à fait conforme aux données actuelles de la littérature et que vous êtes totalement d'accord avec la

proposition, Les valeurs comprises entre « 2 » et « 8 » traduisent les situations intermédiaires possibles, La

valeur « 5 » correspond à votre indécision. Nous vous demandons d'accompagner d'un commentaire toutes

les propositions pour lesquelles vous le jugez nécessaire et obligatoirement pour toute note inférieure à 5. Il

est  important  d'éviter  les  données  manquantes  :  si  vous  êtes  indécis,  il  est  préférable  de  coter  «  5  »  plutôt

que de ne pas répondre. Vous avez aussi la possibilité de signaler que la question est hors de votre champ

de  compétences  («  Je  ne  peux  pas  répondre  »).  Nous  attirons  votre  attention  sur  le  fait  que  seules  les

versions  finales  des  documents  seront  diffusées.  Celles-ci  pourront  être  modifiées  par  rapport  à  celles  que

nous  vous  transmettons.  De  ce  fait,  nous  vous  remercions  de  respecter  toute  confidentialité  et  de  ne  pas

diffuser ces documents. La date limite de réponse à ce questionnaire est fixée au 25 septembre 2025 délai de

rigueur.  Nous  vous  remercions  de  votre  collaboration  à  ce  projet  et  restons  à  votre  disposition  pour  toute

information complémentaire ou question technique.

pourquoi ne parler que de l'entésopathie ossifiante (et non calcifiante) du LAC et ne pas mentionner d'éventuelles

Commentaires

calcifications

aucun intérêt

ne pas mélanger les choses. Il faut décrire soit des calcifications = dépôts d'hydroxyapatite (rares mais possible dans

un contexte de rupture) soit des ossification d'enthèse en particulier du LAC (et là il s'agit d'un tissu osseux)

Calcifications des parties molles en général, pas seulement du LAC

et calcification péri articulaire, notamment dans le cadre de la demande de reconnaissance en maladie professionnelle

(tableau 57)

et calcifications tendineuses éventuelles

Remplacer le terme "calcification" par "ossification"

"Ossification" plus fréquente que "calcification" du LAC en radiographie

tout dépend ce que l'on recherche

Je suis en accord sur le fait d'intégrer la présence de calcification du moment que l'on accompagne cette description

d'un avis sur une corrélation ou non avec la symptomatologie clinique. En effet, une grande partie (certains chiffres

parlent de 50 à 70%) des calcifications sont asymptomatiques et découvertes de manière fortuites (Louwerens, 2015,

10.1016/j.jse.2015.02.024; Sansone, 2016, 10.1007/s00256-015-2240-3)

Attention à la terminologie agressive.

Une majeure partie des arthropathies acromio-claviculaires sont asymptomatiques.

Dès lors, la mention du caractère hypertrophique de l'articulation suffit.

Le terme "agressif" sous-entend un lien de causalité mécanique avec une éventuelle symptomatologie sous

acromiale qui est loin d'être systématique là encore.

D'autre part, il s'agit d'un terme nocébogène, pouvant augmenter le sentiment de nécessité de recourir à la chirurgie

Barreto, R. P. G., Braman, J. P., Ludewig, P. M., Ribeiro, L. P., & Camargo, P. R. (2019). Bilateral magnetic

resonance imaging findings in individuals with unilateral shoulder pain. Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery,

28(9), 1699-1706. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jse.2019.04.001

Lluch-Girbés, E., Dueñas, L., Struyf, F., Camerone, E. M., & Rossettini, G. (2025). Negative expectations and related

nocebo effects in shoulder pain: a perspective for clinicians and researchers. Pain Management, 15(2), 93-104.

https://doi.org/10.1080/17581869.2025.2467022

Le terme "agressif" ne me semble pas adapté, au sens où il n'explicite pas clairement un état patho-anatomique

mais risque engendrer, d'une part des attentes plus fortes envers la chirurgie quand bien même elle ne serait pas

nécessairement indiquée (Zadro JR, O'Keeffe M, Ferreira GE, Traeger AC, Gamble AR, Page R, Herbert RD, Harris

IA, Maher CG. Diagnostic labels and advice for rotator cuff disease influence perceived need for shoulder surgery:

an online randomised experiment. J Physiother. 2022 Oct;68(4):269-276. doi: 10.1016/j.jphys.2022.09.005. Epub

2022 Oct 17. PMID: 36257876), et d'autre part, des attentes très négatives, et donc générer des effets nocebo, chez

les patients qui prendraient connaissance du compte-rendu (Lluch-Girbés E, Dueñas L, Struyf F, Camerone EM,

Rossettini G. Negative expectations and related nocebo effects in shoulder pain: a perspective for clinicians and

researchers. Pain Manag. 2025 Feb;15(2):93-104. doi: 10.1080/17581869.2025.2467022. Epub 2025 Feb 20. PMID:

39973297; PMCID: PMC11853614).

Ces descriptions anatomiques d'articulation acromio-claviculaires "agressives", d'acromion "agressif" ou de "conflit

sous-acromial" ne sont pas corrélées à la symptomatologie clinique et sont des termes perçus comme extrêmement

nocebo par les patients. Ces effets nocebo impactent les parcours de soins, favorisent le catastrophisme et le

sentiment de gravité et d'incurabilité, augmentent les recours à la chirurgie et diminuent le recours aux soins non

invasifs. (Zadro, 2021, 10.2519/jospt.2021.10375; Lewis, 2025, 10.2519/jospt.2025.13405, Zadro, 2O22,

10.1016/j.jphys.2022.09.005, Brindisino, 2025, 10.3389/fresc.2025.1624056, Lluch-Girbes, 2025,

10.1080/17581869.2025.2467022)

pertinente.

suspicion de composante traumatique la présence d'un hypersignal évoquant un œdème par contusion, associée à

un important épanchement sous acromial est un élément important. Vous n'évoquerez pas non plus l'hypersignal

musculaire qui accompagne certaines ruptures traumatiques ou une atteinte neurone (diagnostic différentiel).

Questionnaire : Modèle de compte-rendu opératoire

Nombre d'experts sélectionnés : 55 personne(s)

Taux de participation : 81.81%

Nous vous remercions d'avoir accepté de participer au groupe de lecture relatif à la « Prise en charge des

tendinopathies rompues de la coiffe des rotateurs : place de la chirurgie ». Vous trouverez ci-dessous le

questionnaire concernant le modèle de compte-rendu opératoire. Votre mission consiste : à lire le texte des

recommandations, l'argumentaire, les modèles de comptes-rendus et la fiche synthétique ; à donner un avis

sur la lisibilité, la faisabilité et l'applicabilité de ce modèle de compte-rendu opératoire en cotant chaque

proposition de recommandations à l'aide de l'échelle de cotation et en apportant des arguments

complémentaires ou contradictoires (sous forme de commentaires libres) reposant si possible sur la

littérature, et sur votre expertise lorsque la littérature est insuffisante ou inexistante. Nous vous invitons à lire

l'ensemble des documents avant de remplir le questionnaire, afin d'avoir une vision globale. De même, nous

vous invitons à répondre en respectant l'ordre du questionnaire (lecture verticale du questionnaire) en raison

de l'interrelation existante entre les différentes propositions des chapitres. Pour la phase de cotation, en

regard de chaque proposition du questionnaire est placée une échelle numérique discontinue graduée de « 1

» à « 9 ». La cotation doit être fondée sur les données de la littérature et votre expérience dans le domaine

abordé. La valeur « 1 » signifie que la proposition n'est pas du tout conforme aux données actuelles de la

littérature et que vous êtes en désaccord total avec la proposition, La valeur « 9 » signifie que la proposition

est tout à fait conforme aux données actuelles de la littérature et que vous êtes totalement d'accord avec la

proposition, Les valeurs comprises entre « 2 » et « 8 » traduisent les situations intermédiaires possibles, La

valeur « 5 » correspond à votre indécision. Nous vous demandons d'accompagner d'un commentaire toutes

les propositions pour lesquelles vous le jugez nécessaire et obligatoirement pour toute note inférieure à 5. Il

est important d'éviter les données manquantes : si vous êtes indécis, il est préférable de coter « 5 » plutôt

que de ne pas répondre. Vous avez aussi la possibilité de signaler que la question est hors de votre champ

de compétences (« Je ne peux pas répondre »). Nous attirons votre attention sur le fait que seules les

versions finales des documents seront diffusées. Celles-ci pourront être modifiées par rapport à celles que

nous vous transmettons. De ce fait, nous vous remercions de respecter toute confidentialité et de ne pas

diffuser ces documents. La date limite de réponse à ce questionnaire est fixée au 25 septembre 2025 délai de

rigueur. Nous vous remercions de votre collaboration à ce projet et restons à votre disposition pour toute

information complémentaire ou question technique

État des pratiquesLes données de cette infographie sont issues d’une étude observationnelle sur le système national des données de santé (SNDS) menée par la HAS sur les patients âgés de 18 ans ou plus opérés entre juillet et décembre 2022 d’une chirurgie réparatrice de la coiffe des rotateurs. Les données ne distinguent pas les ruptures de coiffe traumatiques et non traumatiques.www.has-sante.frJuin 2026Chirurgie réparatrice de la coiffe des rotateurs Des parcours de soins qui peuvent s’améliorerLa HAS a fait le point sur l’état des pratiques en menant une étude sur les parcours de soinsdes patients adultes avant et après chirurgie réparatrice de la coiffe des rotateurs.Une chirurgie généralement faite par arthroscopie94 %avec un acte associé(acromioplastie, arthroplastie acromio-claviculaire et/ou ténodèse/ténotomie du biceps)93 %par arthroscopie≈ 26 000patients adultes opérés      au second semestre 202270 % des patientsn’ont pas eu de traitement                  médico-fonctionnel complet(kinésithérapie et infiltration)33 % des patientsn’ont pas eu la combinaison           radiographie et imagerie en coupe (IRM, arthro-IRM ou arthroscanner)Une prise en chargepréopératoire* incomplète...* Dans les 18 mois précédant l’intervention... mais un taux de rééducation postopératoire** satisfaisant94 % des patientsont eu de la kinésithérapieen libéral et/ou hospitalisationen SMR** Dans les 6 mois suivant l’interventionAméliorer la prise en charge autour de la chirurgie réparatrice de la coiffe des rotateursPoints clés de la recommandation 2026 yLa rupture traumatique sur tendon sain est à différencier de la rupture dégénérative. Elle nécessite un avis chirurgical sans délai, en particulier chez le sujet actif. yLe traitement médico-fonctionnel des épaules douloureuses par rupture dégénérative est à réaliser pendant au moins 6 mois avant de discuter une indication chirurgicale (si une gêne fonctionnelle ou une douleur invalidante persistent). yL’imagerie préopératoire comprend une radiographie de l’épaule (faces 3 rotations et faux profil de Lamy) et une imagerie en coupe (IRM, arthroscanner ou arthro-IRM). yEn cas d’indication chirurgicale, la réparation anatomique du tendon est la technique de référence. Elle est réalisée le plus souvent par voie arthroscopique. Les gestes associés à la réparation ne sont pas systématiques. yEn cas d’indication chirurgicale, la rééducation est indispensable en pré et en postopératoire. Le protocole de rééducation et de réadaptation dépend de l’intervention réalisée. Elle nécessite une collaboration entre le masseur-kinésithérapeute et le chirurgien, ainsi qu’un partage d’informations.Pour en savoir plus

## p_4391652 : 2023-09-19_synthesis_-_diagnostic_management_of_non-traumatic_shoulder_pain_in_adults

RECOMMENDING BEST PRACTICES
TOOLKIT GUIDE
Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults
Validated by the HAS Board on 31 August 2023
Key messages
 Degenerative rotator cuff lesions are not always expressed clinically.
 Clinical assessment and evaluation of the context (work or other) are essential for diagnostic and therapeutic management.
Subacromial pain syndrome is non-traumatic shoulder pain, usually unilateral, localised around the tip of the shoulder (and which may radiate down the arm), often exacerbated during or after raising the arm. This syndrome includes the following diagnoses: bursitis, rotator cuff tendinopathy and degener-ative rotator cuff tears, long head of biceps tendinopathy and calcific tendinitis (EC).
The acromioclavicular joint is anatomically close to the rotator cuff. Acromioclavicular joint disease is a common condition that should not be overlooked (EC).
The term “subacromial pain syndrome” should be preferred to:
‒ “scapulohumeral periarthritis”, which should no longer be used and should be considered to be obsolete (EC);
‒ “subacromial impingement”, which is considered to be one of the contributing factors in this multifactorial condition (EC);
‒ “rotator cuff tendinitis” (EC).
Diagnosis of shoulder pain present for less than six weeks (acute)
The four diagnoses to be considered in the event of non-traumatic acute shoulder pain by order of frequency (EC):
‒ Episode of acute pain due to degenerative rotator cuff tendinobursitis: context of repetitive movements
‒ Acute hyperalgesia of the shoulder = calcification in the resorption phase. Intense and sudden shoulder pain without any triggering factor, active and passive mobilisation almost impossible because of the pain. Patient showing signs of upper limb trauma

‒ Shoulder pain with prolonged morning stiffness: context of chronic inflammatory arthritis or known microcrystalline disease = arthritis/bursitis secondary to an acute episode of chronic inflammatory arthritis or microcrystalline arthritis
‒ Parsonage-Turner syndrome: intense, sudden shoulder pain, followed by muscular atro-phy of one or more muscle groups in the shoulder girdle and upper limb
It is also essential to perform a clinical assessment (interview and physical examination) to investigate for urgent diagnoses (EC).
Table 1. Urgent diagnoses to be considered in the event of recent non-traumatic shoulder pain (EC)
Diagnosis
History (context and suggestive symptoms)
Cardiovascular disease (acute coronary
syndrome, ischaemic heart disease, peri-
carditis, aortic dissection, etc.)
− Cardiovascular risk factors
− Chest pain, dyspnoea
Pulmonary embolism
− Risk factors for deep-vein thrombosis
− Chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis
Septic arthritis
− Immunosuppression, intravenous drug use
− Local or remote portal of entry, prolonged morning stiffness, insom-
nia, fever, chills, deterioration in general health
Polymyalgia rheumatica associated with
signs of giant-cell arteritis (Horton disease)
− Age > 50 years
− Pain in the shoulders, bilateral from the outset, pelvic girdle involve-
ment, prolonged morning stiffness, unusual headaches, deterioration
in general health, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness
Apical lung cancer
− Active or previous smoking
− Cough, haemoptysis, Horner’s syndrome, deterioration in general
health
Pleurisy, pneumonia, pneumothorax
−  Chest pain, dyspnoea, cough, fever
Bile duct disease, liver disease, peritoneal
disease (post-surgical irritation)
−  Hypochondrial pain, vomiting, jaundice

Diagnosis of shoulder pain present for more than six weeks (persistent)
The main diagnoses of shoulder pain are sought on the basis of the clinical presentation (EC).

Clinical assessment is routinely supplemented by investigation for any of the main differential diagnoses (EC).
Diagnosis
Patient history
Shoulder tumour
− Deterioration in general health, palpation of a mass
C5 or C6 cervicobrachial neuralgia
− Neuropathic pain, posterior radiation, cervical spine syndrome, abnormal
neurological examination
Post-herpetic neuralgia (C5-C6-T1 der-
matome)
− Neuropathic pain, history of vesicular skin rash “in patches” along the
dermatome pathway
Thoracic outlet syndrome
− Neuropathic pain, absence of cervical spine syndrome, positional nature,
positive challenge test. May be associated with vascular signs
Spinal cord conditions (syringomyelia,
myelitis, cervical spondylotic myelopa-
thy, etc.), motor neurone disease
− Neuropathic pain, abnormal neurological examination
Clinical assessment of shoulder pain
Clinical assessment is essential to make a diagnosis and includes:
‒ a shoulder-specific interview specifying the circumstances of pain onset, the context (work-re-lated or other), the rhythm (possible position-related night-time awakening in subacromial pain syn-drome), the intensity of the pain, the functional impact, etc. (EC). It is important to note that pain in the scapula area is more suggestive of a spinal origin (EC);
‒ inspection of the patient, without clothes, to look for muscular atrophy and assess the position of the scapula during active movements (EC);
‒ bilateral palpation of the acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints (EC);
‒ systematic study of joint ranges of motion on active and passive mobilisation, which must be bilateral and comparative (part of this mobility is not related to the glenohumeral joint). The ranges of motion to be assessed are (diagrams in order of the ranges of motion cited) (EC):
- flexion (anterior elevation) (physiological value 170°-180°),
- abduction in the plane of the scapula (oblique at 30° in front of the frontal plane) (physiological value 170°-180°),
- lateral rotation with elbow to body (also called lateral rotation in position 1 (LR1)) (variable physio-logical value, compare the patient’s two sides),
- medial rotation with hand behind back (also called medial rotation in position 1 (MR1)) (variable physiological value, compare the patient’s two sides, but physiological differences depending on the side).

In the absence of neurological damage, a combination of complete passive mobility and deficient active mobility points towards rupture of one or more rotator cuff tendons (EC).
The presence of joint stiffness, particularly on lateral rotation and abduction, is suggestive of capsulitis or gleno-humeral joint disease (EC);
‒ a neurological assessment of the shoulder and upper limbs (including muscle testing) and an examination of the cervical spine (EC).
Specific physical examination for shoulder pain without stiffness
It is recommended to perform a combination of tests (since these tests have a low diagnostic value), with some pointing to subacromial pain syndrome and others indicating the location of the lesion (EC). Diagnosis of sub-acromial pain syndrome is based on a range of factors (EC).
The following tests can be used to point towards subacromial pain syndrome (EC) (carry out several of these tests to increase the sensitivity and specificity of the clinical assessment):
‒ painful arc test: the patient must perform an abduction movement (in the frontal plane). Pain gen-erally appears at between 60 and 120° of abduction;
‒ Neer test: passive (between flexion and abduction) flexion (anterior elevation) of the upper limb, scapula held in place;
‒ Hawkins test: the arm is placed at a flexion (anterior elevation) angle of 90° (elbow bent to 90°) by the examiner. The examiner imposes medial rotation;
‒ Yocum test: the patient places their hand on the opposite shoulder to the one being tested. They raise their flexed elbow without moving the shoulder being tested.
These tests are positive in the event of the onset of pain during the movement. The tests with a green back-ground are passive and those with a blue background are active for the patient.
The tests making it possible to locate a specifically damaged tendon are (EC):
‒ tests reproducing the pain (in favour of tendinopathy) (low diagnostic value):
- supraspinatus: Jobe test: the arm is at 90° of abduction in the plane of the scapula in medial rotation (thumb downwards). The patient must resist the downward pressure exerted by the exam-iner.
- infraspinatus: Patte test: the arm is at 90° of abduction, elbow bent at 90° and held in place by the examiner, The patient performs a lateral rotation movement against resistance,
‒ long biceps: Palm-up test: the upper arm is positioned at 90° of flexion, with the forearm in supi-nation. The patient must resist the downward pressure exerted by the examiner;

‒ tests for muscle weakness (suggestive of rupture) (EC), description of the most usual and most studied tests:
- supraspinatus: Jobe test,
- infraspinatus:
o Patte test or
o lateral rotation against resistance in position 1 (LR1 against resistance) : the elbow is held against the body, flexed at 90°. The patient must perform a lateral rotation movement against resistance by the examiner,
- subscapularis:
o Gerber test (also called lift-off test): the back of the patient’s hand is against their back, with the elbow flexed at 90°. The patient must move their hand away from their back or
o Belly-press test: the elbow is flexed at 90°; the forearm is in the frontal plane and the hand on the abdomen. The patient presses the abdomen and tries to keep their forearm in the frontal plane. There is subscapular muscle weakness (positive test) if the elbow moves back-wards when the wrist is flexed or
o Bear-hug test: the patient places the palm of their hand on the opposite shoulder to the one being tested, with the fingers straight and the elbow against the front of the body. The patient must maintain the initial position, despite the lateral rotation (applied perpendicularly to the forearm) exerted by the examiner.

This document presents the main points of the publication:
Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults
, “Clinical practice guideline” method, August 2023 All our documents are available to download at

## p_4391653 : 2023-09-19_synthesis_-_management_of_rotator_cuff_tendinopathies

RECOMMENDING BEST PRACTICES
TOOLKIT GUIDE
Management of rotator cuff tendinopathies
Validated by the HAS Board on
31 August 2023
Updated on
Jan 2024
Key messages
 The main treatment is medical and functional: analgesics, NSAIDs, physiotherapy, cortico-steroid injection, education and advice (including advice on personal and professional pre-vention).
 To date, injections of hyaluronic acid or platelet-rich plasma have not demonstrated their efficacy on subacromial pain syndrome.
 Standard X-rays can eliminate a number of differential diagnoses. It is essential that these be performed as a first-line approach (after pain has been present for four to six weeks). The decision to prescribe an ultrasound or MRI will be made on the basis of the clinical reassessment.
 Referral to a shoulder specialist (rheumatologist, physical medicine and rehabilitation spe-cialist, sports medicine specialist or orthopaedic surgeon) is useful if symptoms do not im-prove.
 In rotator cuff tendinopathy, in the absence of a full-thickness tear, surgery has not been shown to provide benefit based on the current evidence and should only be considered after failure of appropriate conservative management, including medical and functional treat-ment.
This toolkit guide concerns the management of non-traumatic, non-hyperalgic rotator cuff disease.

Methods
Grade
First
line
Advice
No immobilisation, continuation of tolerable activities, maintenance of work activities depend-
ing on constraints and functional limitation
EC
Paracetamol, combined or otherwise with step 2 analge-sics depending on the intensity of the pain
Special precautions in patients over 75 years of age:
− the maximum recommended paracetamol dose is 3 g/d in elderly patients weighing over
50 kg. For patients with a lower bodyweight, the paracetamol dosage should be adjusted
downwards on the basis of their weight;
− step 2 analgesics should be prescribed with caution, due to the risk of adverse effects;
− to limit the risk of iatrogenic effects, treatment via injections may be preferable to systemic
treatment in a context of multiple health conditions.
EC
NSAIDs, in the event of acute pain, in combi-nation with anal-gesics
At anti-inflammatory doses, as a short course of treatment, in the absence of contraindications,
in combination with PPIs
1
 if necessary.
It is essential to assess the risk/benefit ratio of prescribing NSAIDs in the elderly. The dosage
should be adapted to the patient's profile and the course should be as short as possible. Sub-
acromial corticosteroid injections may be preferable in these patients.
B
Second
line
Physiotherapy
A physiotherapy programme requires at least:
− an initial assessment (physiotherapy diagnostic assessment);
− active recentring of the humeral head;
− progressive strengthening of the rotator cuff and shoulder muscle complex (scapulotho-
racic and deltoid muscles);
− work to recover and/or maintain joint range of motion;
− manual therapy, in combination with other active techniques;
− work to correct the posture of the spine and shoulder girdle;
− sensorimotor – proprioception training or neuromuscular control;
− teaching patients to implement a self-rehabilitation programme;
− work to combat kinesiophobia and other factors predictive of a poorer response.
The pace, duration and frequency of sessions should be adapted to the evolution of symptoms
and regularly reassessed. A clinical improvement is expected after six weeks to three months.
B
Subacromial corticosteroid injections
Shoulder X-rays must be performed before injection.
The choice of the corticosteroid injected is left to the operator’s discretion, in line with the mar-
keting authorisations of products for peri-articular injection. The choice of method (approach,
volume injected, clinical or imaging identification) is left to the operator. An interval of at least
three weeks must be left between two injections. An injection report must be produced.
A subacromial injection can be performed in patients on antiplatelet drugs or VKAs (if INR < 3,
to be checked before the procedure)
2
. As regards direct oral anticoagulants: for procedures
involving a risk of minor bleeding, such as rheumatology injections, a good practice sheet sug-
gests interrupting treatment for 24 hours before the procedure and resuming it at least six
hours after the end of the invasive procedure, in the absence of any particular haemorrhagic
event.
3
 Collaboration with the physician having prescribed the anticoagulant is essential. Other
guidelines on the management of direct oral anticoagulants during invasive procedures have
been published, but without any consensus.
After a corticosteroid injection, increased monitoring of blood sugar levels should be scheduled
in patients with diabetes.
B

## p_4391654 : 2023-09-19_guideline_-_diagnostic_management_of_non-traumatic_shoulder_pain_in_adults_and_management_of_rotator_cuff_tendinopathy

RECOMMENDING
BEST PRACTICES
GUIDE
Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy
Validated by the HAS Board on
 31 August 2023

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 2
Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are defined in healthcare as systematically developed statements to assist practitioner and patient decisions about appropriate healthcare for specific clinical circumstances.
CPGs are rigorous summaries of the state-of-the-art and scientific data at a given time, described in the evidence report. They do not exempt healthcare professionals from exercising discretion in the patient's treatment; this must be the treat-ment considered to be most appropriate on the basis of their own findings and the patient’s preferences.
These clinical practice guidelines were developed according to the method summarised in the evidence report and in the HAS methodological guide available online: Development of best practice guidelines – Clinical practice guidelines method.
The objectives of this guideline, the population and the professionals concerned by its implementation are summarised (information sheet) and described in detail in the evidence report.
The latter and the guideline summary can be downloaded from www.has-sante.fr.
Grades of recommendations
A
Established scientific evidence
Based on studies with a high level of evidence (level of evidence 1): randomised controlled trials with high power and without major bias or meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, decision analysis based on well con-ducted studies.
B
Scientific presumption
Based on scientific presumption provided by studies with an intermediate level of evidence (level of evidence 2) such as low power randomised controlled trials, well conducted non-randomised controlled studies, cohort stud-ies.
C
Low level of evidence
Based on studies with a lower level of evidence such as case-control studies (level of evidence 3), retrospective studies, case-series studies, comparative studies with major biases (level of evidence 4).
EC
Expert consensus
In the absence of studies, the recommendations are based on agreement between experts in the working group after consultation of the review group. The absence of grading does not mean that the recommendations are not relevant and useful. However, it should prompt additional studies.

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 3
Description of the publication
Title
Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy
Working method
Development of best practice guidelines “Clinical practice guidelines” method (updated in 2020)
Objective(s)
To answer the following questions:
− What elements of the clinical assessment help guide the diagnosis in the event of shoulder pain (investigation for signs of tendinopathy, capsulitis, osteoarthritis)?
− On the basis of which elements should an imaging exam be prescribed, and which exam?
− What is the treatment for rotator cuff tendinopathy without a tear?
Targets
All healthcare professionals liable to treat these patients, including, in particular: general practitioners, rheumatologists, physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists, sports med-icine specialists, geriatric medicine specialists, orthopaedic surgeons, radiologists, occupa-tional health specialists and physiotherapists.

CNAMTS [French National Health Insurance fund for salaried workers]/DDGOS [Depart-ment for the Management and Organisation of Care]/DAS[Department of Social Ac-tion]/Department for Care Coordination and Efficiency

1. Glossary
The anatomical terms used in the guideline adopt the new anatomical nomenclature.
This glossary links the new and the old terms:
Flexion = anterior elevation or antepulsion
Infraspinatus = subspinatus
Lateral rotation = external rotation
Medial rotation = internal rotation

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 6
2. Definition
Subacromial pain syndrome is non-traumatic shoulder pain, usually unilateral, localised at the tip of the shoulder (and which may radiate down the arm), often exacerbated during or after raising the arm. Micro-injuries are included in the topic covered (EC).
This syndrome includes the following diagnoses: bursitis, rotator cuff tendinopathy and degenerative rotator cuff tears (particularly of the supraspinatus), long head of biceps tendinopathy and calcific ten-dinitis. For tendon tears, the partial/full-thickness characteristics relate to thickness of the tendon dam-age and the complete or not characteristics to the sagittal dimension (width) of the tendon (EC).
The term “subacromial pain syndrome” should be preferred to:
‒ “scapulohumeral periarthritis”, which should no longer be used and should be considered to be obsolete (EC);
‒ “subacromial impingement”, which is considered to be one of the contributing factors in this multifactorial condition (EC).
The rotator cuff consists of four muscles: the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the teres minor and the subscapularis. Theoretically, the long head of biceps tendon is not part of the rotator cuff, but its ana-tomical and functional proximity justifies inclusion of conditions affecting this tendon in the wider context of rotator cuff disorders (EC).

3.2. Non-traumatic persistent shoulder pain (present for > 6 weeks)
An initially acute shoulder condition can persist for more than 6 weeks. Other diagnoses should also be considered, depending on the patient’s clinical presentation (Table 3):
‒ shoulder pain with little or no limitation of movement on passive mobilisation (EC):
• shoulder pain with little or no limitation of movement on active and passive mobilisation,
• shoulder pain with limitation of movement on active mobilisation but not on passive mobili-sation (at most pseudoparalysis);
‒ shoulder stiffness = limitation of movement on passive mobilisation (EC);
‒ shoulder instability (demonstrated episodes of repeated dislocation or subjective symptoms of instability (apprehension)) (EC);
‒ neurological shoulder pain: presence of muscular atrophy (EC).

In the event of persistent shoulder pain, the arguments in favour of subacromial pain syndrome are:
‒ the site of the pain: localised in the great majority of cases over the tip of the shoulder and potentially radiating down the arm. Localised pain over the scapula are more suggestive of a spinal origin (EC);
‒ the absence of stiffness: a painful shoulder without stiffness is a shoulder in which range of motion is preserved on passive mobilisation. However, in patients with the most severe shoulder pain, a moderate decrease in overall passive range of motion may be observed (EC);
‒ clinical tests in favour of subacromial pain syndrome (EC).
Subacromial pain syndrome can cause position-related night-time awakening (decubitus) (EC).
Subacromial pain syndrome is often associated with neck conditions (EC).
Clinical assessment is routinely supplemented by investigation for any of the main differential diagno-ses (Table 4).

4. Clinical assessment
A clinical assessment is the first step in the patient’s management and includes: a patient interview, inspection, bilateral palpation of the acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints, examination of ranges of motion on active and passive mobilisation, specific tests, examination of the cervical spine and neurological examination. This assessment must systematically be bilateral and comparative (EC).
The shoulder-specific interview details the location of the pain, the circumstances of its onset, the rhythm, intensity, length of time it has been present, the perceived reduction in shoulder range of mo-tion, the dominant limb, the patient’s socioprofessional status and context, level of physical activity, risk factors, trauma history, treatments undertaken, functional impact (limitation of personal and profes-sional activity) and participation restrictions (disability) (EC).
Shoulder pain and function (activity limitation) can be assessed using a questionnaire validated in French, such as DASH (Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand). The Constant score (already recommended by the HAS but not validated in French before surgery) and the SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index) (not validated in French) are frequently used. These scores document the evolu-tion of symptoms under treatment (EC).
During an inspection of the patient, without clothes, from the back and then the front, the posture is examined, looking for muscular atrophy of the supraspinous and/or infraspinous fossae (suggestive of an old tear of the supraspinous and/or infraspinous tendons or a neurological disease), muscular atro-phy of the deltoid and swelling of the anterior aspect of the arm (Popeye’s sign, suggestive of a long head of biceps rupture). It is also necessary to systematically look for any asymmetries in the osteoar-ticular contours (in particular acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular) and the position of the scapula during active movements (EC).
A bilateral study of ranges of motion on active and passive mobilisation is systematically per-formed (part of this mobility is not related to the glenohumeral joint). The study of ranges of motion during passive mobilisation can be facilitated by performing the examination with the patient in the supine position. The ranges of motion to be assessed are (diagram in order of the ranges of motion cited) (EC):
‒ flexion (anterior elevation) (physiological value 170°-180°);
‒ abduction in the plane of the scapula (i.e. oblique at 30° in front of the frontal plane) (physiolog-ical value 170°-180°);
‒ lateral rotation with elbow to body (also called lateral rotation in position 1 (LR1)) (variable phys-iological value, compare the patient’s two sides);
‒ medial rotation with hand behind back (measured by the distance between the C7 spinous pro-cess and the MCP2 or by the level of the vertebra under MCP2, but this is not pure medial rotation: it also involves glenohumeral extension and elbow flexion, in particular) (also called medial rotation in position 1 (MR1)) (variable physiological value, compare the patient’s two sides, but physiological differences depending on the side).

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 12
In the absence of neurological damage, a combination of complete passive mobility and deficient active mobility points towards rupture of one or more rotator cuff tendons. A shoulder with pseudoparalysis (normal passive elevation with active elevation < 90°) is suggestive of massive rotator cuff rupture (EC).
There are numerous tests to assess rotator cuff condition. Some point to subacromial pain syndrome and others indicate the location of the lesion (by looking for pain, weakness or both), with variable diagnostic values (generally low). These tests should not be used in isolation but in combination. Diagnosis is based on a range of factors (EC).
The following tests can be used to point towards subacromial pain syndrome (EC) (carry out several of these tests to increase the sensitivity and specificity of the clinical assessment):
‒ painful arc test: the patient must perform an abduction movement (in the frontal plane). Pain generally appears at between 60 and 120° of abduction;
‒ Neer test: passive (between flexion and abduction) flexion (anterior elevation) of the upper limb, scapula held in place;
‒ Hawkins test: the arm is placed at a flexion (anterior elevation) angle of 90° (elbow bent to 90°) by the examiner. The examiner imposes medial rotation;
‒ Yocum test: the patient places their hand on the opposite shoulder to the one being tested. They raise their flexed elbow without moving the shoulder being tested.
The diagrams with a green background are passive and those with a blue background are active for the patient.
These tests are positive in the event of the onset of pain during the movement.

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 13
The tests make it possible to locate a specifically damaged tendon (EC):
‒ reproduction of pain (in favour of tendinopathy) (low diagnostic value):
• supraspinatus: Jobe test: the arm is at 90° of abduction in the plane of the scapula in medial rotation (thumb downwards). The patient must resist the downward pressure exerted by the examiner.
• infraspinatus: Patte test: the arm is at 90° of abduction, elbow bent at 90° (also called position 2) and held in place by the examiner. The patient performs a lateral rotation move-ment against resistance,
• long biceps: Palm-up test: the upper arm is positioned at 90° of flexion (anterior elevation), with the forearm in supination. The patient must resist the downward pressure exerted by the examiner.
• to date, no test has been evaluated for the assessment of non-ruptured subscapularis tendinopathy;
‒ testing for muscle weakness (suggestive of rupture), description of the most usual and most studied tests (EC):
• supraspinatus: Jobe test,
• infraspinatus:
- Patte test, or
- lateral rotation against resistance in position 1 (LR1 against resistance): the elbow is held against the body, flexed at 90°. The patient must perform a lateral rotation move-ment against resistance by the examiner,
• subscapularis:
- Gerber test (also called lift-off test): the patient holds the back of their hand against their back, with the elbow flexed at 90°. The patient must move their hand away from their back, or
- Belly-press test: the elbow is flexed at 90°; the forearm is in the frontal plane and the hand on the abdomen. The patient presses the abdomen and tries to keep their forearm in the frontal plane. There is subscapular muscle weakness (positive test) if the elbow moves backwards when the wrist is flexed, or
- Bear-hug test: the patient places the palm of their hand on the opposite shoulder to the one being tested, with the fingers straight and the elbow against the front of the body. The patient must maintain the initial position, despite the lateral rotation (applied perpendicu-larly to the forearm) exerted by the examiner.

5. Imaging in the event of non-hyperalgic, non-traumatic shoulder pain without stiffness
Imaging cannot be prescribed without a prior clinical assessment. The results of the examinations performed should be explained to the patient by the physician (EC).
As a first-line approach, it is useful to perform X-rays on the symptomatic shoulder (anteroposterior views in neutral, internal and external rotation as well as a Lamy false-profile view) (if necessary bilat-eral and comparative, in the absence of data on the value of systematic bilateralism), to look for calcification and a differential diagnosis of rotator cuff disease. These X-rays are indicated if there is no improvement in symptoms after four to six weeks, with or without treatment (most shoulder pain evolves favourably within this time) (EC). In the absence of any new clinical events, there is no indica-tion to repeat the X-rays (EC).
If treatment combining physiotherapy and injection fails, after clinical reassessment, an ultrasound of the shoulder (bilateral and comparative if necessary), carried out by an ultrasound technician experienced in osteoarticular conditions
4
 (i.e. regularly performing osteoarticular ultrasound exams) may be prescribed to specify the diagnosis of the lesion (full-thickness, superficial or deep tear, bursitis, active calcification with an unusual location, lesion of the long biceps tendon
5
 and its environment, acromioclavicular joint disease or other intra-articular disease (synovitis, chondromatosis, etc.)) and adapt therapeutic management (EC).
An MRI (unless contraindicated), carried out by a radiologist experienced in osteoarticular conditions, may be prescribed if the patient's symptoms are not explained by an ultrasound exam, if there is a strong suspicion of tendon rupture and/or if there is no experienced ultrasound technician available. An MRI can look for a full-thickness rotator cuff tear and assess its extension and muscle trophicity (EC).
Ultrasound or MRI should only be prescribed if a radiographic assessment has been performed be-forehand (EC).
A CT or MRI arthrogram is indicated if there is any doubt about the diagnosis on MRI, if there is any radioclinical dissociation or if surgery is indicated. These examinations are prescribed by the specialist taking care of the patient (EC).
A CT scan without arthrography of the shoulder is of no use unless prescribed by a specialist (in addi-tion to an MRI showing a suspicious tumour lesion, calcification or post-traumatic bone lesion in par-ticular) (EC).
In the event of a surgical decision, the type of preoperative imaging is left to the surgeon's choice (EC).
4 To date, there is no regulatory definition of an ultrasound technician experienced in osteoarticular conditions.
5 In most cases, effusion around the tendon of the long biceps is a continuation of glenohumeral effusion and is not sufficient in itself to make a diagnosis of long biceps tenosynovitis.

6. Management of non-traumatic, non-calcific rotator cuff tendinitis
6.1. Analgesics
During the initial phase of treatment, as a first-line approach and depending on the intensity of the pain, analgesics (paracetamol, combined or otherwise with step 2 analgesics (WHO classification)) are rec-ommended. These medications should be periodically reassessed (EC). The efficacy of analgesics on subacromial pain syndrome has not been assessed in the literature.
Special precautions in patients over 75 years of age:
‒ the maximum recommended paracetamol dose is 3 g/d in elderly patients weighing over 50 kg. For patients with a lower bodyweight, the paracetamol dosage should be adjusted downwards on the basis of their weight (maximum 60 mg/kg/d) (EC);
‒ step 2 analgesics should be prescribed with caution, due to the risk of adverse effects. They should be introduced with caution, taking into account comorbidities and associated polymedi-cation, as well as any history of adverse reactions with these analgesics (EC);
‒ to limit the risk of iatrogenic effects, treatment via injections may be preferable to systemic treat-ment in a context of multiple health conditions (EC).
Non-hyperalgic subacromial pain syndrome does not require shoulder immobilisation (EC).
Time off work is not systematic but should be adapted to the patient's job (EC).
6.2. Anti-inflammatories
6.2.1. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
In the event of acute pain, NSAIDs may be used in combination with analgesics, at anti-inflammatory doses, as a short course of treatment, in the absence of contraindications, due to their efficacy in terms of alleviating pain (Grade B). Concomitant prescription of a proton pump inhibitor and an NSAID is only useful in patients with a risk factor for peptic ulcer disease (see good practice sheet for proton pump inhibitors).
6
In patients over 75 years of age, it is essential to assess the risk/benefit ratio of prescribing NSAIDs, due to the increased risk of adverse effects in these patients (risk of iatrogenicity and drug interactions). The dosage should be adapted to the patient's profile and the course should be as short as possible.
7
 Subacromial corticosteroid injections may be preferable in these patients (EC).
6.2.2. Oral corticosteroids
In the absence of scientific evidence of a favourable benefit/risk ratio, oral corticosteroids should not be used in non-calcific rotator cuff tendinitis (EC).

6.3. Subacromial corticosteroid injections
In patients with persistent subacromial pain syndrome, subacromial corticosteroid injections (in com-pliance with contraindications) are useful, since they have a pain-relieving effect that lasts three to eight weeks (Grade B).
Shoulder X-rays must be performed before injection to eliminate any differential diagnosis (EC).
A local anaesthetic may be injected at the same time (EC).
To date, no method (approach, volume injected, clinical or imaging identification) has been shown to be superior, and the choice of method is left to the operator (Grade B).
One or two injections into the shoulder, at least three weeks apart, may be performed depending on the evolution of symptoms and the efficacy of the first injection (Grade B), followed by 48 hours' relative rest, adapted to the patient's work situation. Strict immobilisation is not necessary after injection (EC). The choice of the corticosteroid injected is left to the operator’s discretion (EC), provided that triamcin-olone hexacetonide (Hexatrione®) and triamcinolone acetonide (Kenacort retard®) are not approved for use in the subacromial bursa.
An injection report (location, technique and product injected) must be produced (EC).
There is no point in repeating injections if there is no lasting improvement (EC).
A subacromial injection can be performed in patients on antiplatelet drugs or VKAs (if INR < 3, to be checked before the procedure)
8
. As regards management of direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban (Eliquis®), dabigatran (Pradaxa®) and rivaroxaban (Xarelto®)): for procedures involving a risk of minor bleeding, such as rheumatology injections, a good practice sheet suggests interrupting treatment for 24 hours before the procedure and resuming it at least six hours after the end of the invasive procedure, in the absence of any particular haemorrhagic event
9
. Collaboration with the physician having pre-scribed the anticoagulant is essential. Other guidelines on the management of direct oral anticoagu-lants during invasive procedures have been published, but without any consensus.
After a corticosteroid injection performed in a diabetic patient, the glucose balance may be disrupted for one to three days and increased monitoring of blood sugar levels should be scheduled in these patients (EC). Corticosteroid injections should be avoided in patients with poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension (although there is no HbA1c threshold that formally contraindicates the performance of an injection) (EC). In patients with poorly controlled comorbidities, the corticosteroid dose should be adapted (EC).
Serious adverse reactions (in particular, infection) are rare in randomised controlled trials (Grade B).
6.4. Hyaluronic acid and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections
To date, injections of hyaluronic acid or PRP have not demonstrated their efficacy on subacromial pain syndrome (Grade B).

6.5. Physiotherapy
A physiotherapy programme requires, at least:
‒ an initial assessment (physiotherapy diagnostic assessment), a summary of which is sent to the prescribing physician (EC);
‒ active recentring of the humeral head (Grade B);
‒ progressive strengthening of the rotator cuff and shoulder muscle complex (scapulothoracic and deltoid muscles) (Grade B);
‒ work to recover and/or maintain joint range of motion (EC);
‒ manual therapy, in combination with other active techniques (EC);
‒ work to correct the posture of the spine and shoulder girdle (EC);
‒ sensorimotor – proprioception training or neuromuscular control (EC);
‒ teaching patients to implement a self-rehabilitation programme (EC);
‒ work to combat kinesiophobia (EC) and other factors predictive of a poorer response.
The pace, duration and frequency of sessions should be adapted to the evolution of symptoms and regularly reassessed via physiotherapy assessments. A clinical improvement is expected after six weeks to three months (after 7 to 15 sessions). An insufficient improvement requires a medical reas-sessment before deciding whether to continue physiotherapy (EC).
Whenever possible, it is advisable to refer the patient to a physiotherapist experienced in shoulder rehabilitation (i.e. regularly carrying out musculoskeletal rehabilitation, particularly on the shoulder)
10
 (EC).
Preparation for resumption of sports activities is possible, depending on the patient’s level of require-ment and activities (EC).
In subjects over 75 years of age, with geriatric profiles, in the event of a loss of autonomy warranting hospitalisation, rehabilitation can take place in a specialised geriatric medical care and rehabilitation department (EC).
Adjuvant therapies may be added, but they have not demonstrated their efficacy in subacromial pain syndrome and cannot constitute the only treatment (EC).
6.6. Surgery
In subacromial pain syndrome, in the absence of a full-thickness tear and following the failure of first-line medical treatment:
‒ there is no evidence of any efficacy of isolated subacromial decompression surgery (acromio-plasty and bursectomy) compared to arthroscopic placebo (Grade A);
‒ data suggest that exercises are just as effective as subacromial decompression surgery com-bined with exercises. Surgery has no added value compared to an exercise programme (Grade B);
‒ to determine the value of subacromial decompression surgery as second-line treatment, it is necessary to assess the risk factors for failure of medical treatment in high-quality studies (EC).
The indications for rotator cuff repair will be covered in a subsequent guideline.
10 The specific nature of the practice is recognised by the French College of Physiotherapy.

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 19
The decision to operate on a patient for degenerative tendinopathy is never an emergency and must be the result of a medical-surgical discussion between the various healthcare professionals involved in the treatment and with the patient (EC).
6.7. The role of shoulder specialists
If well-managed first-line conservative treatment (taking into account professional or other contextual factors) fails, it is advisable to seek the advice of a physician or surgeon specialising in shoulder con-ditions (rheumatologist, physical medicine and rehabilitation specialist, sports medicine specialist, or-thopaedic surgeon) (EC).
In complex situations, it is advisable to schedule a multidisciplinary approach that may involve several healthcare professionals: physician/surgeon, rehabilitation specialist (physiotherapist, occupational therapist, psychomotor therapist, etc.), other professionals (psychologist, social worker, adapted phys-ical activity trainer, sports trainer, etc.) (EC).
6.8. Prevention and repair
6.8.1. Prevention
Regular physical activity helps prevent musculoskeletal disorders of the upper limb (EC).
Working conditions and risk factors should be assessed by the physicians treating the patient, in con-junction with the occupational health physician (EC).
The physician treating the patient may advise the patient to contact the occupational health physician, particularly in the context of a pre-return to work visit or a visit that has been requested in order to assess job-related constraints in the workplace (physical, psychological and organisational) and to put in place adaptations and adjustments designed to improve working conditions (EC).
If working conditions have contributed to the development of the tendinopathy, in order to avoid recur-rences and therapeutic failures and to keep the patient in employment, it is necessary to schedule consideration of demonstrated occupational risk factors and potential job-related cofactors at an early stage (EC) (low level of evidence):
‒ repeated or sustained activity with the arms raised above shoulder level;
‒ heavy lifting;
‒ work-related psychosocial factors (high work pressure, job dissatisfaction, organisational fac-tors).
However, the efficacy of managing these risk factors on the incidence and prevalence of rotator cuff tendinopathy has not been demonstrated in the literature.
6.8.2. Social management
Rotator cuff tendinopathy without a tear, linked to repetitive strain, may be recognised as a compen-sable occupational condition (see Table 57 of occupational diseases and conditions), with the excep-tion of calcific tendinitis (Molé radiological classification type A, B and C calcifications, but not insertion calcifications or calcifications seen only on ultrasound (EC)). Rotator cuff tendon tears (partial or full-

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 20
thickness) can be recognised as compensable professional conditions, even in the presence of calci-fications.
In the specific case where the patient, in agreement with the physician, wishes to apply for recognition of an occupational condition, an MRI scan is indicated.
6.9. Patient education
Simple education is recommended for all subacromial pain syndromes, by all healthcare professionals involved in their management (EC). There are virtually no studies on the subject, so the best principles cannot be highlighted (EC).
As with certain complex chronic pain conditions (such as chronic low back pain), therapeutic education for patients with subacromial pain syndrome could prove beneficial, although it is not currently recog-nised in the official specifications (EC).

HAS • Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy • August 2023 21
