## p_4391655 : 2023-09-19_guideline_-_management_of_rotator_cuff_tendinopathy_with_a_tear_-_the_role_of_surgery

RECOMMENDING BEST PRACTICES
SHEET
Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery
Adopted by the HAS Board on 2 July 2026
Main points
 There is not just one type of rotator cuff tear, but several. Each rotator cuff tear must be described in detail (torn tendon(s), partial or full-thickness tear, traumatic, degenerative or mixed aetiology, progression, etc.).
 The clinical presentation of degenerative rotator cuff tears is variable and may change over time.
 A traumatic tear in an otherwise healthy tendon must be distinguished from a degenerative tear. It requires immediate surgical assessment, particularly in active patients.
 Medical and functional treatment of shoulder pain caused by a degenerative tear should be carried out for at least 6 months before considering surgery (if functional impairment or de-bilitating pain persists).
 Consequently, not all tears, even full-thickness ones, require surgery.
 Preoperative imaging includes an X-ray of the shoulder (anteroposterior views in three ro-tations and a Lamy false-profile view) and cross-sectional imaging (MRI, CT arthrogram or MRI arthrogram).
 Where surgery is considered, a specialist consultation is recommended.
 Before determining whether surgery is indicated, the patient is assessed holistically and their biopsychosocial context is taken into account. Complex cases are treated using a mul-tidisciplinary approach.
 Where surgery is indicated, anatomical tendon repair is the gold-standard technique. It is most often performed arthroscopically. Associated procedures performed with the repair are determined on a case-by-case basis.
 Where surgery is indicated, rehabilitation is essential both pre- and postoperatively. The rehabilitation protocol depends on the specific procedure performed. It requires collabora-tion between the physiotherapist and the surgeon, including information sharing (particularly the surgical report and postoperative precautions). Self-rehabilitation plays a key role during the first 3 months.
 Imaging is not routinely carried out postoperatively, unless there is an unfavourable out-come.

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      2
Definitions
The rotator cuff (Figure 1) is a musculo-tendinous complex that dynamically stabilises the gleno-humeral joint; from front to back, at their humeral insertions, it comprises the subscapularis, suprasp-inatus, infraspinatus and teres minor tendons. The anatomical and functional proximity of the long head of the biceps tendon justifies inclusion of conditions affecting this tendon in the wider context of rotator cuff disorders.
Figure 1. Rotator cuff in a sagittal view passing through the humeral head
A rotator cuff tear is a break in the continuity of the tendon (either of the tendon body or at the inser-tion). This injury may be partial or full-thickness and may be caused by trauma or degeneration (or a combination of both: a degenerative injury that has been secondarily aggravated by trauma) (EC).
A partial tear is a break in continuity of the tendon that does not involve the entire thickness of the tendon (EC). It may be:
‒ superficial or “bursal” if it affects the part in contact with the subacromial bursa (Figure 2a);
‒ deep or joint-related if it affects the part in contact with the joint capsule (Figure 2b);
‒ interstitial or intratendinous if it affects the central part of the tendon (Figure 2c).
a    b         c
Figure 2. Examples of different types of partial tears in a frontal section of the shoulder – a: superficial partial tear; b: deep partial tear; c: interstitial partial tear.

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      3
A full-thickness tear (Figure 3) is a break in continuity through the entire thickness of the tendon, connecting the glenohumeral joint to the subacromial bursa. It may affect all or part of the width of the tendon (EC).
                 a               b
Figure 3. Full-thickness tear – a: front view cross-section of the shoulder showing the supraspinatus tendon; b: top view, showing a U-shaped tear.
A special case is delamination (Figure 4), which is an extensive partial interstitial tear of the tendon, associated with a tear in another tendon, which may be either a full-thickness or partial-thickness tear. It most commonly affects the infraspinatus (interstitial tear) (EC).
Figure 4. Delamination of the infraspinatus and full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus, viewed in axial cross section of a left shoulder.
A recent traumatic tendon tear in a healthy tendon is diagnosed based on a range of factors (EC):
‒ Clinically (EC):
- a violent, clearly identified trauma that is biomechanically plausible, such as a dislocation, retropulsion of the arm, axial traction, and/or a violent impact to the arm during a fall and
- the sudden onset of symptoms in a previously asymptomatic patient and
- transient disability;
‒ Imaging (EC):
- a standard X-ray of the shoulder showing no abnormality
- an MRI scan of the shoulder, with or without a prior ultrasound scan (performed as soon as possible after the injury), to look for:
o an absence of fatty infiltration on T1-weighted images
o hemarthrosis, subacromial or intra-articular effusion
o muscle oedema on T2-weighted images
o a distended, wavy appearance of the proximal part of the injured tendon

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      4
o oedema of the greater tubercle indicating a possible avulsion of the supraspinatus
o the persistence of a tendon stump on the greater tubercle
o a thickened tendon (more than 6 mm).
Special case: it is possible for a traumatic tendon tear to occur alongside degenerative changes in another tendon. A healthy tendon may form part of a rotator cuff that is not healthy (EC).
A massive tear is defined as a full-thickness tear involving at least two tendons across their entire width, regardless of the degree of retraction and the condition of the muscle (EC).
An irreparable tear is a tear that cannot be repaired surgically or where repair is doomed to failure due to specific morphological characteristics of the tendons, muscle size and muscle trophicity (EC).
A retear is a tear occurring in a tendon that has already been repaired (EC).
General management principles
1
As a reminder, the clinical assessment of the patient is essential for both diagnosis and treatment. This includes, in particular, specific questioning about the shoulder, visual inspection, palpation and assess-ment of joint range of motion (both active and passive) in both shoulders, a neurological examination of the upper limbs, an examination of the cervical spine and a combination of tests. Pain and function may be assessed using approved questionnaires in French (such as the Western Ontario Rotator Cuff Index, for example).
The first-line treatment for painful shoulders caused by degenerative lesions, with or without a tear, is medical and functional. As a reminder, initial treatment includes:
‒ continuing with activities that can be tolerated (EC);
‒ analgesics (paracetamol ± step 2) ± NSAIDs (unless contraindicated) (EC);
‒ education about the condition, advice and reassurance (EC);
‒ management of loss of independence in older people (EC).
If symptoms persist beyond 4 to 6 weeks, following X-rays of the painful shoulder:
‒ adjust pharmacological treatment (EC);
‒ start physiotherapy (Grade B);
‒ consider administering one or two corticosteroid injections into the shoulder (Grade B)(spaced at least 3 weeks apart, with details recorded in the report). Repeating injections is not recom-mended if there is no lasting improvement.
It is advisable to allow at least one month between the last corticosteroid injection and surgery, given the increased risk of infection and the need for revision surgery (Grade C).
1 HAS 2023 “
Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy
”

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      5
Which imaging should be prescribed preoperatively?
As a reminder,
2
 the first-line examination for a painful, non-traumatic shoulder with no stiffness is a standard shoulder X-ray (EC). If pain persists despite medical and functional treatment, and following clinical reassessment, a shoulder ultrasound scan may be performed (EC). An ultrasound scan is ef-fective at detecting tears when performed by a trained operator but is not sufficient to determine the need for surgery (EC).
Where surgery is indicated, cross-sectional imaging should be performed:
‒ MRI is the gold-standard cross-sectional imaging technique for the rotator cuff. As a minimum, the sequences to be performed are a T1-weighted sagittal sequence without fat saturation (be-yond the Y-slice) and a T2-weighted sequence with fat saturation (three planes: frontal, axial and sagittal). The patient’s shoulder should be in a neutral position (EC);
‒ As a last resort, a CT arthrogram or MRI arthrogram may be performed when there is uncertainty regarding the type of lesion (deep partial tear), the degree of retraction, or when combined with a glenohumeral corticosteroid injection (EC). A CT arthrogram is useful where MRI is contrain-dicated and for assessing the cartilage. At the specialist’s request, different rotations may be performed if necessary to optimise the results of a CT arthrogram (EC).
A CT scan without intra-articular injection is not indicated for the preoperative assessment of rotator cuff tears (EC).
The request for cross-sectional imaging must be justified by the prescribing physician, who will have examined the patient beforehand. The results of any imaging tests already carried out (in particular ultrasound) must be specified on the request form (EC).
In the surgical management of rotator cuff tears, the patient must therefore have (at a minimum) stand-ard X-rays of the affected shoulder (anterior view in neutral rotation, lateral and medial views, and a Lamy false-profile view) and appropriate cross-sectional imaging (EC). The patient is entitled to receive their imaging report and to have easy access to their imaging (EC).
Similarly, the decision to operate is made following a clinical assessment and an analysis of the images and the radiology report. The surgeon cannot determine the need for surgery based solely on the imaging report. It is essential that the healthcare professional examining the patient is able to view the images in the standard axial, frontal and sagittal planes. This forms part of the wider issue of interpret-ing and ensuring continuous access to imaging data (EC).
What are the indications for surgery?
If the patient is experiencing symptoms due to a traumatic tear:
‒ in the case of a healthy tendon (a healthy rotator cuff before the injury, or damage to a previously healthy tendon in a degenerative rotator cuff), a surgical opinion should be sought without delay (Grade C);
‒ in the case of a degenerative tendon, medical and functional management (analgesics, physio-therapy and corticosteroid injection) should be the first-line treatment. Management will then follow the same approach as for degenerative tears (EC).
2 HAS 2023 “
Diagnostic management of non-traumatic shoulder pain in adults and management of rotator cuff tendinopathy
”

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      6
In the case of a tear in a degenerative tendon, the need for surgery should only be considered after at least 6 months of medical and functional treatment. The patient should be referred to an orthopaedic surgeon if, following properly managed medical and functional treatment, the following symptoms per-sist (the areas to be assessed are taken from the Constant score) (EC):
‒ pain (frequency and intensity rated on a numerical scale of 0 to 10) considered significant by the patient;
‒ need for assistance with or inability to resume day-to-day, work-related or leisure activities;
‒ the extent to which the arm can be used without pain in the neck or below;
‒ disabling loss of strength.
In this case, the patient should be referred to a surgeon, regardless of:
‒ their age, if they are active and have functional demand: an active patient over 75 years of age may experience functional improvements following surgery, but the risk of retear is higher than for those under 75 (Grade C);
‒ whether the tear is full-thickness or partial (if the partial tear involves more than 50% of the thickness of the torn tendon) (Grade C);
‒ the size of the tear if it is full-thickness (EC) (although the risk of retear is higher in cases of extensive tearing (Grade C));
‒ the number of torn tendons (EC).
The contraindications to direct anatomical repair of the rotator cuff are:
‒ capsular stiffness (Grade C) (overall range of motion: anterior elevation 90° – lateral rotation 0° – passive medial rotation to the level of the buttock);
‒ advanced radiographic glenohumeral osteoarthritis (glenohumeral joint space narrow-ing), whether primary or secondary (Grade C);
‒ a subacromial space < 6 mm on an anteroposterior shoulder X-ray in neutral rotation (which most often corresponds to full involvement of at least two tendons) (Grade C) (for degenerative tears only);
‒ significant muscle atrophy and/or fatty infiltration of grade > 2 (Goutallier or Fuchs classi-fication, i.e. at least as much fat as muscle) (Grade C).
The factors used to guide the decision to perform rotator cuff repair surgery in other cases are (EC):
‒ clinical tolerance;
‒ the patient’s request and motivation;
‒ the presence of factors associated with a poor prognosis (smoking, obesity, diabetes);
‒ the progression of the lesions;
‒ the size of the lesion (in the frontal and sagittal planes);
‒ a tendon stump length of < 15 mm;
‒ tendinous retraction of more than 5 cm or to the level of the glenoid.
The decision to operate is based on a range of factors. An asymptomatic shoulder should not be op-erated on but should be monitored. The indication for surgery is based on clinical findings (EC).

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      7
The surgeon discusses the indication for surgery based on the clinical assessment (see Constant score) and recent imaging (EC).
Where anatomical repair is not feasible, specialised and sometimes multidisciplinary management is offered. Other surgical techniques may also be discussed with the patient (including biceps tenot-omy/tenodesis, bursectomy, tendinous transfer, patch repair and reverse shoulder arthroplasty) (EC).
Preoperative consultation and occupational context
In all cases, before determining whether surgery is indicated, the patient is assessed holistically. It is particularly important to take the patient’s psychological, social and work context into account. A pre-operative consultation is designed to provide the patient with informed and personalised information on the natural progression of their condition, as well as the expected benefits and risks of rotator cuff repair surgery. The consequences of the surgery (immobilisation, rehabilitation) are assessed (partic-ularly in patients with disabilities) and explained to the patient. Biopsychosocial factors that may con-tribute to chronic post-operative pain and poor physical recovery must be identified (biopsychosocial assessment) and the patient must be informed of these prior to surgery. Referral to appropriate prac-titioners (psychologists, etc.) may be offered to the patient during the perioperative period (EC).
The objectives of the surgery must be defined prior to the procedure, along with the minimum duration of sick leave and the patient’s workplace goals. For patients who are in employment, a pre-return-to-work assessment
3
 is required and must be arranged starting in the fourth month after surgery to plan for any necessary adjustments. The patient must be informed of this and should contact their occupa-tional physician early on (EC).
Manual workers who have undergone rotator cuff surgery are generally on sick leave for more than 6 months (EC).
Early return to work, in a role that has been adapted where necessary, is encouraged (EC).
In complex situations, it is advisable to pursue a multidisciplinary approach that may involve several healthcare professionals: physician/surgeon, rehabilitation specialist (physiotherapist, occupational therapist, psychomotor therapist, etc.) and other practitioners (psychologist, social worker, adapted physical activity trainer, sports trainer, etc.) (EC).
Rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear, confirmed by MRI, may be recognised as an occupational illness (Table 57A). These patients often present with more complex cases, but the fact that the condition is an occupational illness is not a contraindication to rotator cuff repair surgery. The indications for surgery remain the same.
Which surgical techniques are preferred?
The principle behind repairing a rotator cuff tendon tear is to reattach the torn tendon to its bony inser-tion using a system of anchors and sutures. Known as an anatomical repair, the procedure is consid-ered the gold standard (EC).
A thorough understanding of the injury (its shape and whether it can be reduced) is necessary to achieve a successful repair (EC).
3
Paragraph 1:
 Pre-return-to-work assessment (Articles R4624-29 to R4624-30 – Labour Code) – Légifrance

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      8
There are two types of surgery available for repairing the rotator cuff:
‒ arthroscopic surgery, which involves repairing the tendons inside the joint without opening it, guided by a camera and using specialised instruments;
‒ open surgery, which involves repairing the tendons under direct visual control.
The literature does not provide evidence of any difference in efficacy between arthroscopic tendon repair and open or mini-open tendon repair (Grade B). The preferred technique is arthroscopy, but open surgery remains an option (EC). As the aim is tendon healing, the surgeon chooses the surgical technique based on their expertise (EC).
The repair can be carried out using a single row (Figure 5a), a double row (Figures 5b and c), edge-to-edge (allowing the repair of retracted but narrow tears) or, in some cases, may be only partial.
          a     b
                                            c
Figure 5. Types of repairs – a: single row; b: double row with medial knots; c: double row without medial knots, with dependent sutures
In the short and medium term, there are no significant differences in the choice of technique between single-row and double-row repairs in terms of pain reduction and restored function (Grade B). However, at 10 years, double-row repairs maintain their functional improvement, whereas this improvement di-minishes with single-row repairs (Grade C). A double-row repair can be used for all tears. For small lesions (< 3 cm), a single-row repair may be used, while ensuring that tension on the tendons is kept to a minimum (EC).
A double-row repair can be performed with or without a medial knot. Double-row repairs with a medial knot carry a specific risk of retear at the myotendinous junction, but this risk remains low (Grade C) (the rates of retear are identical with or without a medial knot).
The tendon repair should be performed without tension (EC). If covering the entire tendon insertion is not possible without excessive tension, it is possible to perform medial reattachment, suture the rotator cuff to itself edge-to-edge, or augment the repair using the intra-articular portion of the biceps (EC).
As with full-thickness tears, partial tears are operated on following the failure of prolonged medical and functional treatment (EC). Surgical repair is performed either by completion and reattachment or by in situ repair (Grade C). Resection of the acromial enthesophyte may be performed at the same time, most commonly in cases of a superficial partial tear (EC).

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      9
What role do associated procedures and adjuvant treatments play?
Biceps tenodesis/tenotomy and acromioplasty are determined on a case-by-case basis. The surgeon assesses whether they are appropriate based on the findings of the damage assessment.
Acromioplasty is not routinely performed during rotator cuff repair, as its benefit has not been proven (Grade B). However, it may allow for better exposure (EC). The shape of the acromion and periopera-tive findings help inform the decision (EC).
Tenotomy and tenodesis of the long head of biceps tendon are often performed. They offer better outcomes in terms of pain relief when the biceps is pathological (EC). The benefit remains to be demon-strated in cases where there is no pain in the biceps during preoperative clinical assessment, and/or where the biceps is found to be healthy perioperatively (Grade C).
Acromioclavicular arthroplasty (resection of the acromioclavicular joint) is not justified as a first-line adjuvant treatment (Grade C).
There is no proven indication for suprascapular nerve release in rotator cuff repair surgery (Grade C).
There are few studies of high methodological quality on the benefits of synthetic or biological reinforce-ments in rotator cuff repairs. Their indication has yet to be defined and does not appear to be indicated in standard repairs (EC).
Tranexamic acid
4
 may be administered intravenously preoperatively to improve visibility during surgery (Grade C).
The efficacy of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has not yet been demonstrated in combination with rotator cuff repair (Grade C).
What are the prognostic factors?
The goal of rotator cuff repair is to restore a pain-free, mobile and strong shoulder, as well as tendon healing (EC). An unhealed rotator cuff may have a good functional score and cause less pain in the short term, but it is at risk of deteriorating in the long term (Grade C). Strength recovery is better when the rotator cuff has healed (Grade C).
Poorer postoperative clinical outcomes are observed in cases of recognised occupational injury (Grade B), diabetes and obesity (Grade C), and stress and depression (Grade C).
Retear or failure to heal may be suspected if pain persists and tendon testing is abnormal, after a minimum period of 6 months and in the absence of any postoperative traumatic event. The best-doc-umented risk factors for retear or failure to heal are:
‒ related to the patient:
- physiological age (Grade C) (the older the patient, the greater the risk of retear)
- the use of tobacco (Grade C)
- diabetes, particularly if poorly controlled (Grade C)
- obesity (Grade C);
‒ related to the rotator cuff:
- fatty infiltration of grade > 2 (Goutallier or Fuchs classification) (Grade C)
- extensive pre-operative tears (Grade C)
4 Off-label use for rotator cuff repair.

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      10
- an acromio-humeral distance < 6 mm (Grade C);
‒ related to the surgical technique:
- single-row repair (as opposed to double-row) (Grade C)
- repair tension (Grade C).
Modifiable risk factors (including socio-occupational factors) should be addressed without delaying sur-gery as a matter of course (EC).
Role of imaging in the postoperative period
Imaging is not routinely performed in the postoperative period (EC).
Any decision to carry out postoperative imaging rests with the surgeon and is performed by an experi-enced radiologist. Postoperative imaging results are reviewed and explained by the surgeon (EC).
Unless there is a specific indication (trauma, suspected septic arthritis, etc.), there is no indication for imaging within the first 3 months after surgery (EC).
Routine shoulder X-rays do not provide any useful information. They may be performed if clinically indicated (especially in cases of persistent pain, stiffness or failure to regain strength) (EC).
If there is an unfavourable outcome following rotator cuff repair, a shoulder ultrasound scan is the preferred method of investigation, to be carried out by an experienced practitioner, combined with a shoulder X-ray. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty based on clinical findings, an MRI or CT arthrogram may be used to supplement the assessment (EC).
An MRI scan of the shoulder is not useful for assessing the repaired rotator cuff until 6 months after surgery (EC).
What rehabilitation is required before and after surgery to repair rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear?
Preoperative physiotherapy
Preoperative physiotherapy is recommended. Its main objectives are to restore shoulder flexibility (symmetrical passive range of motion), to teach the patient how to use the shoulder brace and perform self-rehabilitation exercises, and to inform them about postoperative care (EC).
A physiotherapy programme includes, in particular (EC):
‒ work to recover and/or maintain shoulder joint range of motion;
‒ training in and assessment of self-rehabilitation exercises to be carried out postoperatively (pen-dulum mobilisation, hands-together exercise, scapulothoracic mobilisation, postural exercises);
‒ progressive strengthening of the periarticular muscles, taking injured tendons into account;
‒ work to correct the posture of the spine and shoulder girdle;
‒ sensorimotor and proprioceptive rehabilitation, and neuromuscular control;
‒ management of kinesiophobia and other factors predictive of a poorer response;
‒ advice (on pain management, wearing the shoulder brace, relaxation) for the patient and their family and friends.

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      11
Postoperative rehabilitation
In all cases, rehabilitation (whether involving physiotherapy and/or occupational therapy) is tailored to the specific procedure performed and to the individual patient. The rehabilitation prescription, drawn up by the surgeon, is specific and detailed and includes, in particular, the guidelines to be followed and precautions to be taken, as well as the various stages of recovery that must be adhered to over time (including the duration of immobilisation and the timeframe for resuming active movement). Any tech-niques that are contraindicated must be specified on the physiotherapy prescription (EC).
Postoperative rehabilitation is carried out in collaboration with the surgeon (EC). The physiotherapist selects the techniques and tailors the rehabilitation programme.
Patients are taught how to perform the self-rehabilitation exercises by the surgeon, supervised by the physiotherapist where necessary (EC). Self-rehabilitation plays a key role during the first 3 months.
In the immediate postoperative period, rehabilitation helps with managing pain, monitoring skin heal-ing, checking posture and ensuring the shoulder brace is correctly positioned. It also helps with moni-toring improvements in joint range of motion and adapting the exercise programmes and self-rehabilitation exercises (ensuring they are pain-free, cautious and progressive). The patient is provided with guidance and advice on managing daily life (EC).
The recommended duration for wearing the postoperative shoulder brace is 4 to 6 weeks, without strict immobilisation (Grade C). The benefits of pendular movement, passive mobilisation followed by imme-diate assisted active mobilisation include a faster recovery of joint range of motion, restoration of the elevation motor pattern, and prevention of stiffness (Grade C). More prolonged immobilisation protects the repair but carries a risk of stiffness (EC).
There is no consensus on the type of shoulder brace to use, although positioning in neutral rotation with the arm abducted seems the most logical approach (Grade C).
To protect the suture, certain movements are contraindicated for 4 to 6 weeks. These must be specified by the surgeon on the physiotherapy prescription and in the surgical report:
‒ no passive lateral rotation (elbow to the body) beyond 0° in cases of subscapularis repair (EC);
‒ no active mobilisation in abduction and in medial rotation combined with extension (EC);
‒ no passive abduction in the strict frontal plane postoperatively (EC).
During the first 6 weeks after surgery, the main areas of focus are (EC):
‒ the gradual recovery of joint range of motion without placing strain on the repair;
‒ the cautious, static reactivation of the rotator cuff muscles;
‒ active mobilisation of the elbow, wrist and hand, and the cervical and thoracic spine;
‒ work to combat pain and kinesiophobia;
‒ gradual weaning off the shoulder brace (after a period determined by the surgeon).
It is advisable to begin with passive (self-passive or assisted active) recovery of joint range of motion, to continue and adapt self-rehabilitation exercises, and then to cautiously begin active rehabilitation without resistance, against gravity.
Between 6 weeks and 3 months after surgery, rehabilitation continues with (EC):
‒ a gradual resumption of active range of motion once passive mobility has been restored as fully as possible;
‒ the restoration of elevation motor patterns;

HAS • Management of rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear: the role of surgery • July 2026      12
‒ proprioceptive exercises while continuing appropriate self-rehabilitation at home.
Normal daily activities without excessive strain will be resumed from the third month onwards (EC).
After 3 months, and as recommended by the surgeon, the aim of physiotherapy is to continue the recovery of active range of motion and to restore muscular balance in the deltoid/rotator cuff muscle pairs. The programme will focus on the gradual resumption of work, sport or leisure activities between 3 and 6 months, focusing on the use of rehabilitation techniques (EC).
From 6 months after surgery, a phase of preparing for the resumption of physical activities may be recommended for manual workers and/or sports enthusiasts (EC).
A more detailed physiotherapy rehabilitation protocol is provided in Appendix 1. This should be adapted to meet the needs of each patient (EC).
A progress report from the physiotherapist must be provided at the postoperative follow-up appoint-ment.
Rehabilitation using hydrotherapy may improve the recovery of mobility in the short term, but its long-term impact is no greater than that of land-based rehabilitation (Grade C). It may be useful as a com-plementary approach, particularly in patients experiencing stiffness or who are anxious or in pain but is not a routine indication (EC).
There is no evidence of the efficacy of shockwave therapy in the postoperative period (Grade C). It is contraindicated (EC).
The occupational therapist has a role to play in managing patients with complex cases. They may also be involved in cases where it is anticipated that returning home will be difficult (particularly when wear-ing an immobilising shoulder brace (EC).
Full recovery is usually achieved one year after surgery (EC). If the prognosis is unfavourable after one year, a specialist consultation is recommended (EC).
Role of medical care and convalescence facilities
Admissions to medical care and convalescence facilities should be considered on a case-by-case ba-sis, whether as day hospital treatment or full hospitalisation (EC).
Some patients with complex cases (especially where surgery has an impact on their psychological and social well-being) may be referred to a medical care and convalescence facility specialising in general or musculoskeletal care (EC).
A medical care and convalescence facility specialising in musculoskeletal care may be useful for pa-tients with high functional goals or requiring coordinated multidisciplinary care (EC).
A medical care and convalescence facility specialising in geriatric care may be useful for patients over the age of 75 who have undergone shoulder surgery, particularly for the most isolated or frail elderly patients. Ideally, elderly patients should receive follow-up care at home after being discharged from hospital. One of the roles of mobile geriatric teams working outside hospitals is to support the patient’s GP in providing care where necessary (EC).

## p_4391658 : 2023-09-19_template_-_essential_information_to_be_included_in_the_surgical_report_for_a_patient_who_has_undergone_surgery_for_rotator_c

RECOMMENDING BEST PRACTICES
SUMMARY
Essential information to be included in the surgical report for a patient who has undergone surgery for rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear
Adopted by the HAS Board on
2 July 2026
The report template provided below must be tailored to each individual patient. It sets out the minimum information to be included in the surgical report on a patient who has undergone surgery for rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear. It may be useful to add further information as appropriate.
The surgical report should be sent to the patient, their general practitioner and all healthcare profes-sionals involved in the patient’s care (with the patient’s consent). The surgical report is added to the patient’s shared medical record after the patient has been informed (the patient may object to this if they have a legitimate reason).
This report template is based on expert consensus.
It is detailed and includes the following elements:
‒ a brief summary of the indication;
‒ the patient’s position during the procedure;
‒ completion of the checklist;
‒ type of anaesthesia administered;
‒ surgical technique: arthroscopic or open surgery, approach;
‒ description of the condition of the cartilage (of the glenoid and the head), the synovial membrane and the subacromial bursa;
‒ description of the condition of each tendon (including the degree of retraction), including the long head of biceps tendon;
‒ description of the repair for each tendon repaired:
• single or double-row, with or without a medial knot,
• number of anchors and their positions, type of anchors (absorbable or non-absorbable) and manufacturer. Traceability of medical devices in accordance with regulations;
‒ percentage of coverage of the greater tubercle or total, partial or medialised repair;
‒ tension (ease of reduction);
‒ possible presence of a leak;
‒ description of the management of the biceps: preservation, tenotomy, tenodesis and type of tenodesis;

HAS • Essential information to be included in the surgical report for a patient who has undergone surgery for rotator cuff tendinopathy with a tear • July 2026      2
‒ description of the management of the acromion and acromioclavicular joint;
‒ any adverse events or complications, including blood transfusions.
The surgical report concludes with recommendations for discharge, including, in particular, instructions and precautions to be followed. The duration of immobilisation, the recommended position and the timeframe before the start of rehabilitation must be specified.

## p_4391659 : 2023-09-19_template_-_essential_information_to_be_included_in_a_preopoerative_imaging_report_for_rotator_cuff_pathology

RECOMMENDING BEST PRACTICES
SUMMARY
Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology
Adopted by the HAS Board on
2 July 2026
The report templates provided below must be tailored to each individual patient. They set out the min-imum information to be included in the preoperative rotator cuff examinations. It may be useful to add further information as appropriate.
It is advisable to write a conclusion that is understandable to both healthcare professionals and pa-tients.
These report templates are based predominantly on expert consensus.

HAS • Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology • July 2026      2
Shoulder X-ray
The shoulder X-ray report must include at least the following elements:
‒ technical conditions: equipment, any specific difficulties relating to the patient, dose adminis-tered;
‒ information provided by the referring practitioner:
• clinical context,
• previous imaging results, treatment history,
• purpose of the request: what is expected from the examination;
‒ side;
‒ views obtained;
‒ assessment of quality criteria for the anteroposterior X-ray (in neutral rotation);
‒ description of bone density (sclerosis, bone demineralisation, focal abnormality);
‒ description of anatomical relationships, if pathological;
‒ measurement of the subacromial space on the anteroposterior view in neutral rotation (shortest distance between the inferior cortex of the acromion and the apex of the humeral head);
‒ appearance of the joint space on the anteroposterior view in neutral rotation (narrowing, pres-ence of osteophytes);
‒ presence or absence of an enthesophyte of the coracoacromial ligament;
‒ presence or absence of tendon calcifications;
‒ presence or absence of hypertrophic changes of the acromioclavicular joint or acromioclavicular osteophytes;
‒ presence or absence of sclerocystic changes of the greater tubercle;
‒ measurement of the CSA (Critical Shoulder Angle).
The conclusion will summarise the results of the X-ray, comparing them with the patient’s symptoms; it will answer the question posed by the referring practitioner and, in the case of a follow-up examina-tion, will note any changes observed.

HAS • Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology • July 2026      3
Shoulder ultrasound
The shoulder ultrasound report must include at least the following elements:
‒ technical conditions: equipment, any specific difficulties relating to the patient;
‒ information provided by the referring practitioner:
• clinical context,
• previous imaging results, treatment history,
• purpose of the request: what is expected from the examination;
‒ side;
‒ presence or absence of signs of tendinopathy for each tendon;
‒ for each torn tendon, a description of:
• the type of tear (full-thickness or partial (superficial, deep or interstitial)), its location and whether or not delamination is present,
• width of the tear in the transverse plane (short axis of the tendon) and the length of the tear in the longitudinal plane of the tendon (long axis of the tendon),
• whether or not tendon fibres are present at the insertion site,
• estimated muscle trophicity (for the supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor) and fatty infiltration, to the extent that this can be assessed by ultrasound;
‒ appearance of the long head of biceps tendon (whether or not there is a tear, its position, thick-ness, presence or absence of peritendinous effusion, and stability or instability during dynamic examination);
‒ presence or absence of glenohumeral or subacromial effusion;
‒ presence or absence of congestive acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular arthropathy, which is painful on examination.
The images must include, as a minimum, cross-sections of each rotator cuff tendon in the long and short axes (with annotations for each image taken), the long head of the biceps tendon and the acro-mioclavicular joint.
The conclusion will summarise the results of the ultrasound, comparing them with the patient’s symp-toms; it will answer the question posed by the referring practitioner and, in the case of a follow-up examination, will note any changes observed. It will also specify whether further imaging is required.
The radiologist explains the results of the examination to the patient.

HAS • Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology • July 2026      4
Shoulder MRI
The preoperative shoulder MRI report must include at least the following elements:
‒ technical conditions: equipment, any specific difficulties relating to the patient;
‒ information provided by the referring practitioner:
• clinical context,
• previous imaging results, treatment history,
• purpose of the request: what is expected from the examination;
‒ side;
‒ sequences performed;
‒ presence or absence of signs of tendinopathy for each tendon;
‒ for each torn tendon, a description of:
• the type of tear (full-thickness or partial (superficial, deep or interstitial)) and its location,
• presence or absence of delamination and its extent,
• width of the tear in the transverse plane (short axis of the tendon) and the length of the tear in the longitudinal plane of the tendon (long axis of the tendon),
• whether or not tendon fibres are present at the insertion site,
• length and appearance of the tendon stump (assessment of the tendon’s thickness and uni-formity, and estimation of retraction using the Patte classification
1
, taking into account the most distal area where the tendon retains its full thickness),
• muscle trophicity (to be measured on a sagittal T1-weighted image of the Y-section (on the most lateral image showing contact between the scapular spine and the scapula) and graded according to the Warner classification
2
),
• degree of fatty infiltration of the muscle (according to the Goutallier
3
 or Fuchs classification
4
);
‒ appearance of the long head of biceps tendon (whether or not there is a tear, its position, thick-ness, presence or absence of peritendinous effusion);
‒ presence or absence of glenohumeral or subacromial effusion;
‒ condition of the glenohumeral cartilage and subchondral bone, and the presence or absence of osteophytes;
‒ description of the morphology and whether or not the acromioclavicular joint appears con-gested;
‒ presence or absence of bone or muscle oedema.
1 The Patte classification describes tendon retraction (particularly of the supraspinatus) on a frontal section of the shoulder in three stages: Stage 1: proximal tendon stump near the bony insertion; Stage 2: proximal tendon stump at the level of the humeral head; Stage 3: proximal tendon stump at the level of the glenoid or more proximal.
2 The Warner classification assesses muscle atrophy in four stages: no atrophy: the muscle completely fills its fossa and the outer contour is convex; minimal atrophy: the outer contour of the muscle is flat compared to its fossa; moderate atrophy: the outer con-tour of the muscle is concave within the fossa; severe atrophy: the muscle is barely visible within its fossa.
3 The Goutallier classification assesses fatty infiltration on the Y-section across five grades: Grade 0: normal muscle; Grade 1: muscle contains some fatty streaks; Grade 2: fatty infiltration is present, but there is more muscle than fat; Grade 3: equal amounts of muscle and fat; Grade 4: more fat than muscle.
4 The Fuchs classification, based on T1-weighted imaging, assesses fat infiltration across three grades: Grade 1: normal muscle containing some fatty streaks; Grade 2: fatty infiltration is present, but there is more muscle than fat; Grade 3: as much or more muscle than fat.

HAS • Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology • July 2026      5
The imaging series must include at least three views (axial, sagittal, frontal) in T2-weighted mode with fat saturation, and one sagittal view in T1-weighted mode, extending at least as far as the origin of the spine on the scapular spine. The images are to be given to the patient.
The conclusion will summarise the results of the MRI, comparing them with the patient’s symptoms; it will answer the question posed by the referring practitioner and, in the case of a follow-up examination, will note any changes observed. It will also specify whether further imaging is required.

HAS • Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology • July 2026      6
Shoulder CT arthrogram
The preoperative shoulder CT arthrogram report must include at least the following elements:
‒ technical conditions: equipment, any specific difficulties relating to the patient, quality of opaci-fication of the joint cavity, contrast medium injected, whether or not an associated injection was performed and the name of the product injected, volume injected of each product, route of in-jection, any difficulties encountered during injection, dose administered;
‒ information provided by the referring practitioner:
• clinical context,
• previous imaging results, treatment history,
• the purpose of the request: what is expected from the examination; whether or not cortico-steroid injection is to be administered at the same time;
‒ side, type of shoulder rotation;
‒ multi-planar reconstructions performed;
‒ for each torn tendon, a description of:
• type of tear (full-thickness or partial (superficial, deep or interstitial)) and its location (note: superficial partial ruptures may not be visualised),
• presence or absence of delamination and its extent,
• width of the tear in the transverse plane (short axis of the tendon) and the length of the tear in the longitudinal plane of the tendon (long axis of the tendon),
• whether or not tendon fibres are present at the insertion site,
• muscle trophicity (to be measured on a sagittal image of the Y-section (on the most lateral image showing contact between the scapular spine and the scapula) and graded according to the Warner classification
5
),
• degree of fatty infiltration of the muscle (according to the detailed Goutallier classification
6
);
‒ appearance of the long head of biceps tendon (whether or not there is a tear, its position);
‒ presence or absence of signs of synovial hypertrophy or foreign bodies;
‒ condition of the glenohumeral cartilage and subchondral bone, and the presence or absence of osteophytes;
‒ presence or absence of acromioclavicular arthropathy.
The imaging must include reconstructions in all three views for each rotation (if performed) and sagittal soft-tissue window images to assess muscle condition.
The conclusion must refer to the indication for the CT arthrogram, summarise its findings in relation to the patient’s symptoms, address the question posed by the referring practitioner, mention any changes observed in the case of a follow-up examination, and state whether a corticosteroid injection was ad-ministered at the same time (including the name of the product injected).
5 The Warner classification assesses muscle atrophy in four stages: no atrophy: the muscle completely fills its fossa and the outer contour is convex; minimal atrophy: the outer contour of the muscle is flat compared to its fossa; moderate atrophy: the outer con-tour of the muscle is concave within the fossa; severe atrophy: the muscle is barely visible within its fossa.
6 The Goutallier classification assesses fatty infiltration across five stages: Grade 0: normal muscle; Grade 1: muscle contains some fatty streaks; Grade 2: fatty infiltration is present, but there is more muscle than fat; Grade 3: equal amounts of muscle and fat; Grade 4: more fat than muscle.

HAS • Essential information to be included in a preoperative imaging report for rotator cuff pathology • July 2026      7
Shoulder MRI arthrogram
The arthro-MRI report will incorporate findings from both the MRI and the CT arthrogram.
